title: Reframing Dark Patterns: 2026 Edition
intro: A retail-heavy follow-up. Six patterns still everywhere in 2026 — and each one fails a basic Nielsen heuristic.

learn.title: Six patterns and their honest versions
learn.text:
• **Consent asymmetry** — “Accept All” big, “Reject” buried → make both equally easy
• **Fake urgency** — a timer that resets on refresh → deadlines only when real
• **False scarcity** — “Only 2 left” that isn't → accurate, verifiable stock
• **Pre-selected opt-ins** → optional opt-ins unchecked
• **Misleading labels** — “View pricing” → a sign-up form → the label says where it goes
• **Forms that punish errors** → keep the input, allow paste, allow undo

try.q: A countdown timer restarts when the page is refreshed. Which pattern is this?
options: Fake urgency
False scarcity
Consent asymmetry
A misleading label

learn.title: Pre-selection is absolute
learn.text:
Calabro's position: **a pre-checked opt-in is a dark pattern even when the team believes users benefit.**

People shouldn't have to undo a choice they never made.

There is no version of “but it's useful for them” that makes the pre-check acceptable.

try.q: The team argues the pre-checked newsletter genuinely benefits users. What is Calabro's position?
options: It is still a dark pattern
It is acceptable if easily unchecked
It depends on the opt-out rate
It is acceptable outside the EU
try.explain: Users shouldn't have to undo a choice they never made.

learn.title: Conversion isn't consent
learn.text:
High acceptance or conversion rates don't prove users wanted the outcome. Observing a behaviour tells you what happened under those conditions — not what people would have chosen freely.

And each of the six patterns breaks a basic heuristic: visibility of status, match with the real world, user control, consistency or error prevention.

try.q: Acceptance of a consent banner is 94%. What does that prove?
options: Only what happened under those conditions
That users are happy with the terms
That the design is clear enough
That the pattern is legally compliant

test.q: How does this edition differ from 2025?
options: It focuses on B2C and retail
It drops the user-control principle
It adds legal analysis of the EU rules
It covers enterprise software instead
test.explain: A retail-heavy follow-up to the 2025 edition.

options: Accepting is easy; refusing is buried
Consent is requested twice
Different users see different terms
Consent can't be withdrawn later

test.q: Which heuristic does a misleading button label break?
options: Match between the system and the real world
Visibility of system status
Error prevention
Flexibility and efficiency of use
test.explain: The label should say where it goes.

test.q: What should a form do when it rejects an entry?
options: Keep the input and allow paste and undo
Clear the field to avoid confusion
Scroll to the top of the form
Disable submission until it is fixed
test.explain: Forms that punish errors are one of the six patterns.

test.q: Who does the article say these patterns hurt most?
options: Disabled users
New customers
Mobile users
Users outside the EU
test.explain: As in the 2025 edition, accessibility is where they break first.
